title: What is ArgoCD — a Kubernetes-native GitOps tool that watches a Git repo containing Kubernetes manifests/Helm charts and continuously syncs the cluster state to match — and what is the difference between ArgoCD (pull-based, runs inside cluster) and traditional CI/CD push (Jenkins pushes to cluster)?
shortTitle: What ArgoCD is and how pull-based GitOps differs from push-based CI/CD

s1_definition.profdef: ArgoCD is a Kubernetes-native, declarative GitOps continuous-delivery tool that runs inside the cluster, watches a Git repository containing Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, or Kustomize overlays, and continuously synchronizes the cluster's live state to match the desired state declared in Git. It is pull-based: the in-cluster controller pulls the desired state from Git and applies it, reporting sync status and health, as opposed to a traditional push-based pipeline where an external CI server such as Jenkins holds cluster credentials and pushes changes into the cluster from outside.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of ArgoCD as an inspector who lives inside each National Bank of India data center. He keeps a copy of the official rulebook (the Git repo) and constantly walks the floor making the setup match the rulebook, and he reports a green light when everything matches and a red light when it does not. The traditional push model is the opposite: an outside contractor (Jenkins) keeps the keys to the data center and drives over to make changes whenever told. Pull-based means the inspector inside reaches out to read the rulebook; push-based means an outsider holds the keys and comes in. The inside inspector is safer because no outsider needs the keys.
s1_definition.oneliner: ArgoCD is an in-cluster GitOps controller that pulls desired state from Git and continuously syncs the cluster to match, which is safer and more resilient than an external Jenkins pushing changes in with cluster credentials.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** ArgoCD is a Kubernetes-native, declarative GitOps continuous-delivery tool that runs inside the cluster, watches a Git repository containing Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, or Kustomize overlays, and continuously synchronizes the cluster's live state to match the desired state declared in Git. It is pull-based: the in-cluster controller pulls the desired state from Git and applies it, reporting sync status and health, as opposed to a traditional push-based pipeline where an external CI server such as Jenkins holds cluster credentials and pushes changes into the cluster from outside.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of ArgoCD as an inspector who lives inside each National Bank of India data center. He keeps a copy of the official rulebook (the Git repo) and constantly walks the floor making the setup match the rulebook, and he reports a green light when everything matches and a red light when it does not. The traditional push model is the opposite: an outside contractor (Jenkins) keeps the keys to the data center and drives over to make changes whenever told. Pull-based means the inspector inside reaches out to read the rulebook; push-based means an outsider holds the keys and comes in. The inside inspector is safer because no outsider needs the keys.

**One line to remember:** ArgoCD is an in-cluster GitOps controller that pulls desired state from Git and continuously syncs the cluster to match, which is safer and more resilient than an external Jenkins pushing changes in with cluster credentials.

sections.s2_technical:
ArgoCD models each deployable unit as an Application custom resource that points at a Git repository, a path and target revision within it, and a destination cluster and namespace. The ArgoCD controller running in the cluster periodically polls or is webhook-notified about the repository, renders the manifests (plain YAML, a Helm chart, or a Kustomize overlay), and compares the rendered desired state to the live cluster state. It then reports each Application as Synced or OutOfSync and as Healthy or Degraded, and its web UI and CLI show a live diff of exactly what differs. With an automated sync policy it applies changes automatically; with prune enabled it deletes resources removed from Git; and with self-heal enabled it reverts manual drift back to the Git state.

The pull-based design is the heart of the difference from traditional CI/CD. In a push model, a CI server like Jenkins runs outside the cluster, authenticates to the cluster with privileged kubeconfig credentials, and runs kubectl apply or helm upgrade to push changes in. This means the external system must hold powerful, long-lived cluster credentials, the cluster's API must be reachable from the CI network, and the deployment is a one-shot imperative action with no ongoing enforcement. In the pull model, the ArgoCD controller lives inside the cluster and reaches outward to read Git, so the privileged credentials stay inside the cluster, the cluster API does not need to be exposed to an external CI system, and deployment is a continuous reconciliation rather than a single push.

This leads to several concrete advantages. Security improves because deploy credentials are not spread to an external CI server and the cluster is not exposed; the blast radius of a compromised CI system shrinks. Resilience improves because reconciliation is continuous: if the cluster drifts, ArgoCD corrects it, whereas a push pipeline only acts when triggered and never notices later drift. Visibility improves because ArgoCD always shows the real sync and health status and the exact diff, so you can see whether the cluster matches Git at any moment. Multi-cluster scale improves because one ArgoCD can manage many clusters by pulling, instead of a CI server needing credentials and network paths to each.

The clean separation is that continuous integration and continuous delivery become distinct concerns. CI — which can still be Jenkins, GitHub Actions, or GitLab CI — builds the image, runs tests, and updates the image tag in the Git repository by committing. ArgoCD then handles delivery by syncing that commit to the cluster. So Jenkins is not eliminated; it is repositioned to do build and test and to write to Git, while ArgoCD owns the act of deploying. A senior nuance is that ArgoCD supports progressive delivery through add-ons like Argo Rollouts for canary and blue-green strategies, supports app-of-apps patterns for managing many applications declaratively, and integrates sync waves and hooks for ordering, so it scales from a single service to an entire platform while keeping Git as the single source of truth.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India wants to replace a Jenkins-pushes-to-cluster pipeline with ArgoCD pulling from Git, to remove external cluster credentials and gain continuous drift correction and clear sync status.

Problem 1 — Jenkins held privileged kubeconfig credentials and pushed with kubectl, a security and blast-radius concern. ArgoCD runs inside the cluster and pulls, so no external system holds cluster keys.

Problem 2 — A push pipeline deploys once and never notices later drift. ArgoCD reconciles continuously and reports Synced or OutOfSync and Healthy or Degraded.

Problem 3 — Teams could not see at a glance whether the cluster matched intent. ArgoCD shows a live diff and status. Our runnable Java simulation contrasts a `PushPipeline` (external, one-shot, holds credentials) with an `ArgoCdController` (in-cluster, continuous pull, reports status). Classes: `Application`, `GitSource`, `PushPipeline`, `ArgoCdController`, and an `ArgoCdDemo` main. Real ArgoCD Application YAML is shown as reference.

##### 4c. ArgoCD Application (YAML reference)

```yaml
# ─── File: manifests/application.yaml ───
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: loan-service
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: banking
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.nbi.in/platform/gitops-repo.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: loan-service              # Helm/Kustomize/plain YAML live here
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: banking
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
    syncOptions: [ CreateNamespace=true ]
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Run the Java simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.argo.ArgoCdDemo

# Real ArgoCD usage
kubectl apply -f manifests/application.yaml
argocd app list
argocd app get loan-service          # shows Synced/OutOfSync + Healthy/Degraded + diff
argocd app sync loan-service         # manual sync (automated policy usually does it)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a loan-service application starting at image tag 2.0.0, demonstrated first under push and then under ArgoCD pull.

Step 1 — In the push model, Jenkins uses an external kubeconfig credential to kubectl apply tag 2.1.0 directly to the cluster. The live tag updates once, but nothing watches for later drift, and the powerful cluster credential lives outside the cluster.

Step 2 — In the ArgoCD model, the controller runs inside the cluster. Its first reconcile finds Git desired tag 2.0.0 equals the live tag, so it marks the application Synced and Healthy.

Step 3 — CI builds and tests a new image and commits tag 2.1.0 to the Git repository. ArgoCD's next reconcile sees Git now wants 2.1.0 while the cluster runs 2.0.0, marks it OutOfSync, and because automated sync is on, pulls and applies 2.1.0, returning to Synced and Healthy — all without any external cluster credentials.

Step 4 — Someone edits the cluster by hand to tag 1.9.0, causing drift and an OutOfSync status. ArgoCD's next reconcile detects the drift and, with self-heal on, restores 2.1.0 automatically.

Step 5 — The final state shows the application Synced and Healthy at 2.1.0, with ArgoCD continuously enforcing the Git desired state from inside the cluster, in contrast to the one-shot push that never noticed drift.

Final output:

sections.s6_takeaway:
ArgoCD is a Kubernetes-native, declarative GitOps continuous-delivery tool that runs inside the cluster, watches a Git repository containing Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, or Kustomize overlays, and continuously synchronizes the cluster's live state to match the desired state in Git. Each deployable unit is an Application resource that points at a repository, a path and revision, and a destination namespace, and ArgoCD renders the manifests, compares them to the live cluster, and reports each application as Synced or OutOfSync and Healthy or Degraded, showing an exact diff in its UI. With an automated sync policy it applies changes, with prune it removes resources deleted from Git, and with self-heal it reverts manual drift automatically.

The core difference from traditional CI/CD is pull versus push. In a push model, an external server like Jenkins holds privileged kubeconfig credentials and runs kubectl apply or helm upgrade to push changes into the cluster from outside, which means powerful long-lived credentials live outside the cluster, the cluster API must be reachable from the CI network, and the deployment is a one-shot action with no ongoing enforcement. In ArgoCD's pull model, the controller lives inside the cluster and reaches out to read Git, so the privileged credentials stay inside the cluster, the cluster API is not exposed to an external system, and deployment is a continuous reconciliation rather than a single push. This makes it more secure because deploy credentials are not spread to an external CI server, more resilient because drift is continuously corrected, and more transparent because sync and health status and the live diff are always visible.

Importantly, this does not eliminate Jenkins — it repositions it. CI still builds the image, runs the tests, and commits the new image tag into the Git repository, and ArgoCD then owns the act of deploying by syncing that commit. In my project at the National Bank of India we moved the loan service from a Jenkins-pushes-to-cluster pipeline to ArgoCD: CI committed the new tag to Git, ArgoCD pulled it and synced the cluster with no external credentials, and when someone edited a resource by hand ArgoCD self-healed it back to the Git state. A senior point I always add is that ArgoCD scales from one service to a whole platform through app-of-apps patterns and sync waves, supports canary and blue-green via Argo Rollouts, and can manage many clusters by pulling — all while keeping Git as the single source of truth.
